lessonTitle: The Pocket Problem: Why Women Need More!
lessonGoal: Explain the practical and symbolic importance of pockets, identify supporting details, and write a clear recommendation using evidence and contrast.

warmUp.title: Warm-up
warmUp.instructions: Read and discuss the warm-up questions with a partner. Share your thoughts on clothing functionality and shopping choices.
questions: What do you usually carry in your pockets, and what makes a pocket useful?
How could clothes look attractive but still be inconvenient to wear?
What would make you decide not to buy an item of clothing?

article.title: The Pocket Problem: Why Women Need More!
article.sourceNote: Original text transcribed from a teacher-provided classroom image. The image credits BBC but does not identify the article or the survey behind the 40% figure.
paragraphs: Have you ever wondered why women’s clothes have fewer pockets than men’s? This question is getting a lot of attention lately, especially with the rise of the #WeWantPockets trend on social media.

Women feel frustrated that their pockets are often tiny or even fake! A recent study showed that 40% of women have picked up clothing in a store only to put it back because it didn’t have real pockets.

Fashion designers are starting to take notice. In recent shows, models strutted down the runway confidently with their hands in deep pockets. Caroline Stevenson, a fashion expert, explained, “Pockets have become a symbolic part of male and female dress.” Designers like Claire McCardell made big pockets popular in the past, knowing they help women feel more independent. Although there has been progress, the battle for pocket equality continues, and many are hopeful change is on the way!

vocabularyInContext.title: Vocabulary in Context
vocabularyInContext.instructions: Study the key vocabulary items below from the reading. Pay attention to the part of speech, English definition, Korean meaning, and example sentence.

items.definition: feeling annoyed and disappointed because you cannot achieve or get something you need
items.sentence: Women feel frustrated when clothing features tiny or fake pockets.

items.definition: not real, made to look like something real in order to deceive or imitate
items.sentence: Some jackets have fake pockets that are sewn shut and cannot hold anything.

items.definition: to start paying attention to something or someone
items.sentence: Fashion designers are starting to take notice of customer demand for real pockets.

items.definition: to walk in a confident, proud, and noticeable way
items.sentence: Models strutted down the runway wearing clothes designed with deep pockets.

items.definition: the long narrow stage that models walk along during a fashion show
items.sentence: Models showed off the new collection as they walked down the runway.

items.definition: in a self-assured way that shows certainty and trust in oneself
items.sentence: The models walked confidently with their hands tucked inside deep pockets.

items.definition: serving as a sign or representation of a larger idea, value, or status
items.sentence: Pockets have become a symbolic part of social equality and personal convenience.

items.definition: able to rely on oneself and make choices without depending on others
items.sentence: Useful pockets allow people to carry their own belongings and feel more independent.

items.definition: the state of having the same rights, status, opportunities, and features
items.sentence: The movement for pocket equality calls for functional designs in all clothing.

items.definition: arriving soon or making progress towards happening
items.sentence: Although challenges remain, many shoppers are hopeful that real change is on the way.

mainIdeaQuestion.title: Main Idea
mainIdeaQuestion.question: MI1. What is the article mainly about?
options: A. Why fashion designers have stopped making clothes with pockets.
B. Why women want useful pockets and how designers are beginning to respond.
C. Why social media is the only influence on clothing design.
D. Why every woman prefers the same style of clothing.
mainIdeaQuestion.explanation: Correct: Option B captures the core theme of the article—explaining women’s frustration with impractical pockets, highlighting social media awareness, and describing how designers are starting to respond. Option A incorrectly claims designers stopped making pockets altogether; Option C overstates social media as the sole factor; Option D falsely claims all women prefer one identical style.

questions.question: RC1. What has helped draw attention to the pocket problem, according to the article?
options: A. A new rule requiring pockets in every garment.
B. A decline in the use of social media.
C. The #WeWantPockets trend on social media.
D. A competition to design the smallest pockets.
questions.explanation: Correct: Option C directly matches Paragraph 1, which states that the question is getting attention 'especially with the rise of the #WeWantPockets trend on social media.' Option A, B, and D describe events not mentioned in the text.

questions.question: RC2. Why do women in the article feel frustrated with their pockets?
options: A. The pockets are often tiny or fake.
B. The pockets are always too deep to use.
C. All shops have stopped selling clothes with pockets.
D. Designers require everyone to carry the same things.
questions.explanation: Correct: Option A aligns with Paragraph 2: 'Women feel frustrated that their pockets are often tiny or even fake!' Options B, C, and D contradict or misstate the text.

questions.question: RC3. What does the article report about the 40% figure?
options: A. Forty percent of designers refused to make clothing with pockets.
B. Forty percent of models put their hands in their pockets.
C. Forty percent of clothing shops sold only fake pockets.
D. A study found that 40% of women had put clothing back because it lacked real pockets.
questions.explanation: Correct: Option D accurately states that 'A recent study showed that 40% of women have picked up clothing in a store only to put it back because it didn’t have real pockets.' Note: This is the article’s reported survey claim and is not an independently verified global statistic.

questions.question: RC4. What detail suggests that designers are beginning to take notice?
options: A. Models stopped appearing in fashion shows.
B. Models walked down runways confidently with their hands in deep pockets.
C. Designers removed pockets from all recent collections.
D. Fashion experts stopped discussing clothing.
questions.explanation: Correct: Option B reflects Paragraph 3: 'In recent shows, models strutted down the runway confidently with their hands in deep pockets.' Options A, C, and D contradict the text.

questions.question: RC5. What does the article connect with Claire McCardell's use of big pockets?
options: A. Making clothing difficult to wear.
B. Requiring everyone to follow one fashion trend.
C. Helping women feel more independent.
D. Replacing clothing stores with social media.
questions.explanation: Correct: Option C directly quotes the textual connection in Paragraph 3: 'Designers like Claire McCardell made big pockets popular in the past, knowing they help women feel more independent.'

questions.question: RC6. What does the final sentence suggest?
options: A. There has been progress, but the issue has not been fully resolved.
B. Pocket equality has already been achieved everywhere.
C. Designers have made no changes of any kind.
D. People no longer expect further change.
questions.explanation: Correct: Option A accurately summarizes the concession and ongoing struggle in the final sentence: 'Although there has been progress, the battle for pocket equality continues, and many are hopeful change is on the way!'

evidenceFromText.title: Evidence from the Text
evidenceFromText.instructions: Answer each question using specific evidence from the text.

prompts.statement: E1. What detail in the article suggests that useful pockets can affect shopping decisions? Explain the connection. Suggested 25–45 words.
prompts.modelAnswer: The article reports that 40% of women in a study put clothing back because it did not have real pockets. This suggests that practical features can influence whether shoppers decide to buy an item.
prompts.compareTip: Ensure you include the 40% study detail from Paragraph 2 and explain how the lack of real pockets led women to put clothing back instead of buying it.

prompts.statement: E2. How does the article connect pockets with independence or meaning beyond appearance? Use two details. Suggested 30–50 words.
prompts.modelAnswer: The article connects Claire McCardell’s big pockets with helping women feel more independent. It also reports Caroline Stevenson’s view that pockets have become symbolic. Together, these details suggest that pockets can matter for reasons beyond appearance.
prompts.compareTip: Identify two distinct details from Paragraph 3: Claire McCardell’s big pockets promoting independence and Caroline Stevenson’s quote that pockets are symbolic.

prompts.statement: E3. What evidence shows progress, and what evidence shows that the problem continues? Suggested 25–45 words.
prompts.modelAnswer: Models appeared on recent runways with their hands in deep pockets, suggesting that designers are responding. However, the final sentence says the battle for pocket equality continues, so the article does not present the problem as solved.
prompts.compareTip: Contrast runway models showing deep pockets (progress) with the final sentence stating that the battle for pocket equality continues (ongoing issue).

languageFocus.title: Language Focus: Grammar & Textual Patterns
languageFocus.topic: Fewer vs. Less, Embedded Questions, and Concession
languageFocus.explanation: In feature writing, writers use precise grammar structures to compare quantities, embed question clauses, report disappointing outcomes, and balance progress with ongoing challenges.
examples: Countable: Women’s clothes often have fewer pockets than men’s clothes.
Uncountable: Tiny pockets provide less space for daily essentials.
Embedded Question: Have you ever wondered why women’s clothes have fewer pockets?
Only to + Verb: She picked up clothing in a store, only to put it back because it lacked real pockets.
Concession: Although there has been progress, the battle for pocket equality continues. (Do not write: Although... but...)
practice: WP1: Write one sentence comparing pocket design using fewer and another using less.
WP2: Combine these ideas using although: "Designers are beginning to respond" and "The pocket problem continues."
WP3: Write a sentence using "only to" to describe the shopping situation in the article.
WP4: Write a two-sentence recommendation: explain a problem and suggest a practical improvement using should.

sections.heading: 1. Fewer vs. Less with Nouns
sections.explanation: Use *fewer* with plural countable nouns (e.g., *pockets*, *garments*). Use *less* with uncountable nouns (e.g., *space*, *fabric*, *money*).
examples: Countable: Women’s clothes often have **fewer pockets** than men’s clothes.
Uncountable: Tiny pockets provide **less space** for daily essentials.

sections.heading: 2. Embedded Question Word Order
sections.explanation: When a question is inside a statement or another question, use statement word order (Subject + Verb), not inverted question order.
examples: Direct Question: Why **do** women’s clothes **have** fewer pockets?
Embedded Clause: Have you ever wondered why **women’s clothes have** fewer pockets?

sections.heading: 3. "Only to + Verb" (Unexpected / Disappointing Result)
sections.explanation: The phrase *only to + verb* introduces an unexpected or disappointing outcome following an initial action.
examples: She picked up clothing in a store, **only to put** it back because it lacked real pockets.

sections.heading: 4. Accompanying Prepositional Phrases & Concession
sections.explanation: Use *with + noun + prepositional phrase* to describe accompanying conditions. Use *although* for concession, but do not combine *although* and *but* in the same clause pair.
examples: Accompanying: Models strutted down the runway **with their hands in deep pockets**.
Concession: **Although** there has been progress, the battle for pocket equality continues. (Do not write: *Although... but...*)

sections.heading: 5. Causative & Verb Patterns (Make / Help)
sections.explanation: Notice the structures: *make + object + adjective* and *help + object + base verb* (or *to + verb*).
examples: Big pockets help women **feel** more independent.

writingPractice.title: Writing Practice
writingPractice.instructions: Complete sentence-level writing practice applying key grammar and text patterns.

prompts.question: WP1. Write one sentence comparing pocket design using fewer and another using less. Suggested 15–35 words in total.
prompts.modelAnswer: Some women’s clothes have fewer pockets than men’s clothes. Tiny pockets provide less space for everyday items.
prompts.compareTip: Check that 'fewer' modifies a plural count noun (pockets) and 'less' modifies an uncountable noun (space, room, fabric).

prompts.question: WP2. Combine these ideas using although: "Designers are beginning to respond" and "The pocket problem continues." Suggested 10–25 words.
prompts.modelAnswer: Although designers are beginning to respond, the pocket problem continues.
prompts.compareTip: Use 'although' at the beginning or middle of the combined sentence without adding 'but'.

prompts.question: WP3. Write a sentence using "only to" to describe the shopping situation in the article. Suggested 15–30 words.
prompts.modelAnswer: A shopper picked up an attractive jacket, only to put it back because it had no real pockets.
prompts.compareTip: Ensure 'only to' introduces the unexpected disappointing result (putting the clothing back).

prompts.question: WP4. Write a two-sentence recommendation: explain a problem and suggest a practical improvement using should. Suggested 25–45 words.
prompts.modelAnswer: Tiny or fake pockets can make clothing inconvenient for people who want to carry everyday items. Designers should offer useful pockets alongside attractive styles so that customers have more practical choices.
prompts.compareTip: Sentence 1 describes the functional problem; Sentence 2 uses 'should' to propose a practical design solution.

writingTask.title: Evidence-Based Recommendation Paragraph
writingTask.prompt: Should fashion designers give greater priority to useful pockets in women’s clothing? Write a 100–140-word recommendation paragraph. State your position, use at least two details from the article, explain why they matter, acknowledge progress or another consideration, and suggest a practical design improvement.
frame: 1. Position Statement: Clear stance on whether designers should prioritize useful pockets.
2. Evidence 1: First detail from the text (e.g., 40% study figure or fake pockets).
3. Explanation 1: Why this evidence matters for daily life or shopping decisions.
4. Evidence 2 & Contrast: Second detail (e.g., runway trends, independence, or symbolic value) + concession (although/however).
5. Practical Recommendation: Concrete suggestion for designers using modal verbs (should/could).
6. Conclusion: Summary linking design functionality with customer choices.
writingTask.modelAnswer: Designers should give greater priority to useful pockets in women’s clothing. According to the article, women feel frustrated when pockets are too small or fake. It also reports that 40% of women in a study put clothing back because it lacked real pockets. This suggests that practical features can influence shopping decisions. The article also connects larger pockets with independence through Claire McCardell’s designs. Although recent runway shows suggest progress, the text says the problem continues. Designers should therefore offer clothing with pockets that can hold everyday items while allowing different styles. Useful pockets would give customers more practical choices. However, the survey’s source and scope should be checked before its percentage is applied to all women.
checklist: Stated a clear recommendation position in the opening sentence.
Included at least two accurate details directly from the article.
Explained why the evidence matters for shoppers or clothing design.
Used contrast or concession words (although, however) to balance progress and ongoing needs.
Proposed a realistic, practical design recommendation using 'should'.
Kept the paragraph strictly between 100 and 140 words.

selfCheck.title: Self-Check Checklist
items: I answered all warm-up and comprehension questions using evidence from the original text.
I identified two distinct details from the text (e.g., the 40% study figure, runway trends, or Claire McCardell).
I used contrast structures like 'although' or 'however' without combining them incorrectly.
I included a practical recommendation using 'should' or 'could'.
My recommendation paragraph meets the 100–140 word requirement (Final Model: 117 words).
I verified my student identity and code before clicking Submit.

It also reports that 40% of women in a study put clothing back because it lacked real pockets. This suggests that practical features can influence shopping decisions. rubric.excellent: Formulates a precise, highly relevant recommendation on clothing functionality that directly addresses the prompt.
rubric.developing: States a clear recommendation position with relevant focus.
rubric.beginning: Presents a vague or incomplete recommendation stance.

rubric.excellent: Seamlessly integrates 2+ accurate details from the text (40% study, runway shows, McCardell) with precise source attribution.
rubric.developing: Includes 2 textual details with basic attribution.
rubric.beginning: Includes 1 detail or relies on unverified personal assertions.

rubric.excellent: Demonstrates flawless command of target patterns (fewer vs. less, although without double-conjunction, embedded questions, modal recommendation).
rubric.developing: Uses target contrast and recommendation structures accurately with minor errors.
rubric.beginning: Attempts contrast structures but shows errors (e.g., using both although and but).

rubric.excellent: Follows a logical progression (Position -> Evidence -> Explanation -> Contrast -> Recommendation -> Conclusion) with effective transitions.
rubric.developing: Well-organized paragraph structure with minor flow gaps.
rubric.beginning: Disorganized sequence making reasoning difficult to follow.

rubric.excellent: Strictly within 100–140 words with accurate spelling, punctuation, and capitalization.
rubric.developing: Within 90–150 words with minor mechanical errors.

teacherNotes: 1. Source Literacy & Attribution: Remind students that 'Source: BBC' on classroom printouts represents the image header, but the specific article URL, survey methodology, and sample population for the 40% study figure are not detailed. Teach students to attribute claims to 'the article' or 'a reported study' rather than stating them as absolute global truths.

2. Practical vs. Symbolic Value: Help students analyze how pockets represent both functional utility (holding items) and social symbolism (independence, equality, freedom from carrying bags). Reference Claire McCardell’s historical contribution in the 1940s.

3. Respectful Classroom Discussion: Keep gender discussions focused on design functionality, ergonomics, and consumer choice. Ensure students of all genders feel comfortable sharing opinions on garment design without making sweeping personal generalizations.

4. ESL Common Errors: Watch for double contrast connectors (*Although... but...*), misuse of *fewer* with uncountable nouns (*fewer space*), and incorrect embedded question word order (*wonder why do clothes have*).

script: Greet the class and direct students to Warm-up questions W1–W3.
Pair students to discuss what items they carry daily and what makes a pocket useful or frustrating.
Conduct a quick 2-minute whole-class poll on whether anyone has ever chosen not to buy an item because it lacked pockets.
Present vocabulary items 1–10 with pronunciation, definitions, and Korean equivalents.
Emphasize *take notice*, *strut*, *symbolic*, and the distinction between *fewer* (countable) and *less* (uncountable).
Clarify that in Stevenson’s quote, *dress* refers to clothing/fashion in general, not just a one-piece dress.
Give students 3 minutes to read the 3-paragraph text silently.
Ask students to complete MI1 (Main Idea MCQ).
Confirm why Option B is correct and review why A, C, and D are incorrect distractors.
Guide students through RC1–RC6, referencing exact paragraph locations for each answer.
Instruct students to complete Evidence tasks E1–E3 in their textareas.
Model how to attribute reported figures (e.g., 'According to the article, a study found 40%...').
Explain *fewer* + plural count noun vs. *less* + uncountable noun.
Demonstrate embedded question word order: *wonder why women’s clothes have...*
Highlight *only to + verb* for disappointing results and *although* for concession without *but*.
Have students draft responses for WP1 (fewer/less comparison), WP2 (although combination), WP3 (only to result), and WP4 (two-sentence recommendation).
Use Check & Compare to let students evaluate their sentences against the model answers.
Provide targeted teacher feedback on structural accuracy.
Review the prompt and 6-step paragraph frame (Position -> Evidence 1 -> Explanation -> Evidence 2/Contrast -> Recommendation -> Conclusion).
Students write their recommendation paragraph in the interactive textarea.
Encourage students to use live word count and run the built-in Writing Check for instant feedback.
Students review Self-Check items 1–6.
Verify student code and name in submission header.
Click Submit to send responses to D1 database / local storage fallback.

sentences.chunkReading: A recent study showed / that 40% of women / have picked up clothing in a store / only to put it back / because it didn’t have real pockets.
sentences.directKorean: 한 최근 연구는 보여주었습니다 / 여성의 40%가 / 매장에서 옷을 집어 들었다가 / 결국 다시 제자리에 놓았다는 것을 / 진짜 주머니가 없었기 때문에.
sentences.naturalKorean: 최근 한 연구에 따르면 여성의 40%가 매장에서 옷을 집어 들었다가 진짜 주머니가 없다는 이유로 다시 내려놓은 경험이 있다고 합니다.
sentences.mustKnowGrammar: only to + v 구문은 기대와 달리 실망스러운 결과를 맞이했음을 나타냅니다.
sentences.feynmanExplanation: 옷을 들었다가(picked up), 주머니가 없어서 실망하고 내려놓았다(only to put it back)는 결과적 표현이에요.

teachingTranscript.english: Sentence 4 features 'only to put it back' expressing a disappointing outcome.
teachingTranscript.korean: 문장 4에는 아쉬운 결과를 표현하는 'only to put it back' 구문이 포함되어 있습니다.

sentences.original: Fashion designers are starting to take notice.
sentences.chunkReading: Fashion designers / are starting / to take notice.
sentences.mustKnowGrammar: are starting to v 진행형으로 변화의 시작을 나타냅니다.
sentences.feynmanExplanation: 디자이너들이 드디어 소비자들의 요구에 관심을 기울이기 시작했다는 짧은 전환 문장입니다.

teachingTranscript.english: This short 6-word sentence transitions the topic from consumer frustration to designer response.
teachingTranscript.korean: 이 6단어로 된 짧은 문장은 주제를 소비자의 답답함에서 디자이너의 반응으로 전환합니다.

sentences.original: In recent shows, models strutted down the runway confidently with their hands in deep pockets.
sentences.chunkReading: In recent shows, / models strutted down the runway / confidently / with their hands in deep pockets.
sentences.directKorean: 최근 쇼에서 / 모델들은 런웨이를 뽐내며 걸었습니다 / 당당하게 / 그들의 손을 깊은 주머니에 넣은 채.
sentences.naturalKorean: 최근 패션쇼에서 모델들은 깊은 주머니에 손을 넣은 채 당당하게 런웨이를 걸었습니다.

mustKnowChunks.chunk: with their hands in deep pockets

sentences.mustKnowGrammar: with + 명사 + 전치사구 구조로 손을 주머니에 넣은 부대상황을 표현합니다.
sentences.feynmanExplanation: 모델들이 주머니에 손을 넣고 당당하게 걸어가는 생생한 모습을 묘사하고 있어요.

teachingTranscript.english: Observe how 'with their hands in deep pockets' visualizes progress on the runway.
teachingTranscript.korean: 'with their hands in deep pockets' 구문이 런웨이에서의 변화를 시각적으로 보여줍니다.

sentences.original: Caroline Stevenson, a fashion expert, explained, “Pockets have become a symbolic part of male and female dress.”
sentences.chunkReading: Caroline Stevenson, / a fashion expert, / explained, / “Pockets have become / a symbolic part / of male and female dress.”
sentences.directKorean: 패션 전문가인 캐롤라인 스티븐슨은 / 설명했습니다 / "주머니는 상징적인 부분이 되었습니다 / 남성과 여성의 의복에서."
sentences.naturalKorean: 패션 전문가 캐롤라인 스티븐슨은 "주머니는 남성과 여성 의복의 상징적인 부분이 되었다"고 설명했습니다.
sentences.mustKnowGrammar: a fashion expert 동격 구문과 직접 인용문이 결합된 구조입니다. dress는 복장 전반을 뜻합니다.
sentences.feynmanExplanation: 전문가의 말을 인용한 문장으로, 여기서 dress는 원피스가 아니라 전체적인 의복을 의미합니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Note that Stevenson's quote forms ONE sentence in the text, and dress refers to general clothing.
teachingTranscript.korean: 스티븐슨의 인용문은 본문에서 하나의 문장을 이루며, dress는 일반적인 의복을 뜻합니다.

sentences.original: Designers like Claire McCardell made big pockets popular in the past, knowing they help women feel more independent.
sentences.chunkReading: Designers like Claire McCardell / made big pockets popular / in the past, / knowing they help women / feel more independent.
sentences.directKorean: 클레어 맥카델과 같은 디자이너들은 / 큰 주머니를 유행시켰습니다 / 과거에 / 그것들이 여성들을 돕는다는 것을 알면서 / 더 독립적으로 느끼도록.
sentences.naturalKorean: 클레어 맥카델과 같은 과거의 디자이너들은 큰 주머니가 여성을 더 독립적으로 느끼게 해준다는 점을 알고 이를 대중화했습니다.

mustKnowChunks.meaning: 주머니가 여성이 느끼도록 돕는다는 것을 알면서 (분사구문)

sentences.mustKnowGrammar: make + 목적어 + 형용사 구조와 help + 목적어 + 원형보어 구조가 둘 다 사용되었습니다.
sentences.feynmanExplanation: 과거 디자이너 클레어 맥카델이 주머니를 통해 여성이 독립감을 느끼도록 도왔다는 역사적 예시입니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Sentence 8 connects pockets with female independence through historical designer Claire McCardell.
teachingTranscript.korean: 문장 8은 과거 디자이너 클레어 맥카델을 통해 주머니를 여성의 독립심과 연결짓습니다.

sentences.original: Although there has been progress, the battle for pocket equality continues, and many are hopeful change is on the way!
sentences.chunkReading: Although there has been progress, / the battle for pocket equality continues, / and many are hopeful / change is on the way!
sentences.directKorean: 비록 진전이 있었을지라도 / 주머니 평등을 위한 투쟁은 계속되며 / 많은 사람들은 희망합니다 / 변화가 진행 중이기를!
sentences.naturalKorean: 비록 약간의 진전은 있었지만 주머니 평등을 위한 노력은 계속되고 있으며, 많은 이들이 변화가 다가오고 있다고 희망적으로 바라보고 있습니다!

mustKnowChunks.chunk: hopeful change is on the way

sentences.mustKnowGrammar: although 양보 절 구조와 관용어구 on the way가 사용되었습니다.
sentences.feynmanExplanation: 진전이 있지만 여전히 노력이 계속되고 있고 변화를 희망한다는 마무리 문장입니다.

teachingTranscript.english: Notice how Although balances recent progress with ongoing efforts, ending optimistically with 'on the way'.
teachingTranscript.korean: Although 구문이 최근의 진전과 지속적인 노력을 균형 있게 다루며 'on the way'로 희망적으로 마무리함을 관찰하세요.

sentenceFrames: Designers should give greater priority to useful pockets because...
According to the article, a study showed that 40% of women...
Although recent runway shows suggest progress, the text emphasizes that...
Therefore, clothing brands could improve functional utility by...
paragraphOutline: Step 1: State clear position on whether designers should prioritize useful pockets.
Step 2: Cite Evidence 1 (e.g. 40% study detail or fake pockets).
Step 3: Explain why this evidence matters for shoppers.
Step 4: Cite Evidence 2 & Concession (e.g. runway progress vs. ongoing struggle).
Step 5: Provide a practical design recommendation using modal 'should'.
Step 6: Conclude with a strong closing sentence.

commonMistakes.mistake: Although designers make progress, but the problem continues.
commonMistakes.correction: Although designers are making progress, the problem continues. (Do not use both although and but together.)

commonMistakes.mistake: Women's clothes have less pockets than men's.
commonMistakes.correction: Women's clothes have fewer pockets than men's. (Use fewer with plural count nouns like pockets.)

commonMistakes.mistake: Big pockets help women to feel more independent.
commonMistakes.correction: Big pockets help women feel more independent. (Use help + object + bare infinitive.)

teacherCorrectionFocus: Ensure *fewer* is used for countable nouns (pockets) and *less* for uncountable nouns (space).
Verify that students cite at least 2 specific details from the text with accurate attribution.
